Consult Summary:
- Telemedicine consult for acute continuous room-spinning vertigo with nausea, tinnitus, and unsteady gait beginning ~2 hours prior; clinician’s working diagnosis: labyrinthitis; symptomatic medication prescribed and in-person evaluation arranged with ED precautions discussed.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Sudden onset dizziness described as room-spinning vertigo; nausea; bilateral ear “buzzing”/tinnitus; feels unsteady on feet (can walk but not straight).
- Timeline: Began ~2 hours before consult while making breakfast; persistent/continuous since onset. Similar brief episode ~1 month ago lasting 5–10 minutes that resolved quickly.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: None specified; not reported as positional.
- Associated symptoms: Nausea; sense of shakiness at onset.
- Pertinent negatives: No limb weakness; no hearing loss; no ear pain or discharge; no fever; no recent viral illness; not yet vomited.

Past Medical History:
- Premature ovarian failure; on hormone replacement therapy (HRT). No surgical history mentioned.

Medications:
- HRT (specific agent/dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Newly prescribed vestibular symptom-relief medication (name not captured): one tablet three times daily for 10 days; route not documented. Can be taken with or without food per clinician.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Mentions husband. Tobacco, alcohol, and other substance use not discussed.

Family History:
- Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded (telemedicine; no formal neuro/ear exam performed).

Investigations:
- None obtained during consult. In-person assessment planned (otoscopic exam; blood pressure check; gait/neurologic assessment).

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Acute vestibular syndrome with continuous vertigo, tinnitus, nausea, and gait unsteadiness. Treating clinician’s impression: labyrinthitis. No focal neurologic deficits reported.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Vestibular neuritis (acute unilateral vestibulopathy): Supports—sudden continuous vertigo with nausea and gait unsteadiness, no hearing loss. Opposes—tinnitus present; no viral prodrome documented.
  - Labyrinthitis: Supports—vertigo with auditory symptom (tinnitus). Opposes—no hearing loss, no otalgia/fever.
  - Posterior circulation event (TIA/stroke): Supports—acute continuous vertigo with unsteady gait. Opposes—no focal deficits (no limb weakness, diplopia, dysarthria), younger age; however, HRT use adds vascular risk. Conflict noted (clinician labeled labyrinthitis; DDx favors vestibular neuritis given absence of hearing loss).

- Issue 1: Acute vertigo with tinnitus (suspected labyrinthitis)
  - Start symptomatic vestibular medication (name not captured): one tablet TID x10 days; route not documented; may take with or without food.
  - Arrange urgent in-person evaluation to examine ears, check blood pressure, and assess gait/neurologic status.
  - Safety-net: Attend Emergency Department for any new limb weakness, sudden severe headache, or if vomiting becomes persistent/violent.
  - Patient instructed to call support to book appointment; prescription sent to Lloyds pharmacy.

- Issue 2: Nausea associated with vertigo
  - Managed with the prescribed vestibular symptom-relief medication.
  - Monitor; seek urgent care if vomiting becomes persistent/violent as above.

- Issue 3: Tinnitus without hearing loss
  - Monitor; assess during in-person otoscopic and audiologic screening if indicated.

- General plan items:
  - Follow-up in the next few days for in-person assessment and to review response to therapy; earlier if red flags occur.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: Vitals; focused neurologic exam (including HINTS if appropriate); otoscopic exam; formal gait assessment; medication reconciliation details (HRT agent/dose/route/frequency not documented); exact name and route of new vestibular medication not captured.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: Treating clinician’s diagnosis is labyrinthitis; DDx ranks vestibular neuritis as slightly more likely due to absence of hearing loss—conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Medication name inaudible/not captured; otherwise history is clear.
